subject: Mathematics
title: Raj's Geometry Adventure
hook: Raj discovers lines and angles hidden in his apartment building.

slides.title: The Discovery
slides.storyContext: Raj looks out his window and sees the edges of buildings. Meera points out that edges are really lines.
slides.inSimpleWords: Lines are straight paths that go on forever.

image.alt: The Discovery — Lines and Angles

slides.title: What is a Line?
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a line on paper with a ruler. She explains that a line has no endpoints and goes on infinitely.

points.label: Definition
points.text: A line is a straight path with no endpoints, extending infinitely in both directions.

slides.inSimpleWords: A line never ends, it keeps going forever both ways.

image.alt: What is a Line? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Line Segment and Ray
slides.storyContext: Raj sees the edge of his table (line segment) and the beam of sunlight (ray) coming through the window.

points.label: Line Segment
points.text: A line segment has two endpoints. Example: the edge of Raj's desk.

points.label: Ray
points.text: A ray has one starting point and extends infinitely in one direction. Example: sunlight from a window.

slides.inSimpleWords: A segment has two ends, a ray has one starting point.

image.alt: Line Segment and Ray — Lines and Angles

slides.title: What is an Angle?
slides.storyContext: Meera opens a book like a door hinge. She says the opening between the pages is an angle.

points.label: Angle
points.text: An angle is formed when two rays meet at a common point called the vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: An angle is the space between two rays meeting at a point.

image.alt: What is an Angle? — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Types of Angles
slides.storyContext: Raj measures different angles at home: the door (90°), a clock hand position (45°), and a stretched rope (180°).

example.problem: Classify these angles: 35°, 90°, 120°, 180°
example.solution: 35° is acute (less than 90°), 90° is right, 120° is obtuse (between 90° and 180°), 180° is straight.

slides.inSimpleWords: Acute angles are small, right angles are corners, obtuse are wide.

image.alt: Types of Angles — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Measuring Angles
slides.storyContext: Meera teaches Raj to use a protractor to measure the angle formed by the book pages.

points.label: Protractor
points.text: A protractor is a tool to measure angles. Place the center on the vertex and read the degree marking.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use a protractor to measure angles in degrees.

image.alt: Measuring Angles — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Finding Angles Around You
slides.storyContext: Raj finds angles in his room: corner of floor (90°), clock showing 3:00 (90°), open notebook (varies).

example.problem: What angle does a clock hand make at 3:00 and 6:00?
example.solution: At 3:00, the angle is 90°. At 6:00, the angle is 180°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Clock hands make different angles at different times.

image.alt: Finding Angles Around You — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Angle Hunt
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to find and classify 5 angles in his home.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Find angles at home: door frame (90°), pencil box lid, scissors opening, window corners.

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around and name the angles you see.

image.alt: Angle Hunt — Lines and Angles

slides.title: Lines and Angles Review
slides.storyContext: Raj summarizes what he learned: lines never end, rays have one start, angles form between two rays.

points.label: Lines
points.text: Infinite straight paths with no endpoints.

points.label: Segments & Rays
points.text: Segments have two endpoints, rays have one.

points.label: Angles
points.text: Formed by two rays meeting at a vertex.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lines, segments, rays, and angles are the building blocks of geometry.

image.alt: Lines and Angles Review — Lines and Angles

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Magic Numbers
hook: Meera finds hidden patterns in numbers while organizing her school supplies.

slides.title: Numbers Everywhere
slides.storyContext: Meera counts her pencils: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. She notices every number is made of pairs.
slides.inSimpleWords: Numbers follow patterns we can discover.

image.alt: Numbers Everywhere — Number Play

slides.title: Even and Odd Numbers
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges pencils in pairs. Some pencils pair perfectly (even), one pencil is left alone (odd).

points.label: Even Numbers
points.text: Numbers divisible by 2 with no remainder: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12...

points.label: Odd Numbers
points.text: Numbers that leave remainder 1 when divided by 2: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11...

slides.inSimpleWords: Even numbers divide by 2 perfectly, odd numbers don't.

image.alt: Even and Odd Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Finding Factors
slides.storyContext: Meera arranges 12 pencils in different rectangular groups: 2×6, 3×4, 1×12.

example.problem: Find all factors of 12.
example.solution: Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 (numbers that divide 12 with no remainder).

slides.inSimpleWords: Factors are numbers that divide another number evenly.

image.alt: Finding Factors — Number Play

slides.title: Multiples
slides.storyContext: Raj notices that if 3 is a factor, then 3, 6, 9, 12, 15... are multiples of 3.

points.label: Multiple
points.text: A multiple of a number is the result of multiplying it by any whole number.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiples are what you get when you skip-count.

image.alt: Multiples — Number Play

slides.title: Multiples and Factors Together
slides.storyContext: Meera asks: if 5 is a factor of 20, then 20 is a multiple of 5.

example.problem: List multiples of 4. Then find which numbers have 4 as a factor.
example.solution: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... Numbers with 4 as factor: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 (same list!).

slides.inSimpleWords: If X is a factor, then numbers it makes are multiples of X.

image.alt: Multiples and Factors Together — Number Play

slides.title: Prime and Composite
slides.storyContext: Meera groups numbers: some (like 2, 3, 5, 7) can only be divided by 1 and themselves (prime). Others (like 4, 6, 8, 9) have more factors (composite).

points.label: Prime
points.text: A number with exactly two factors: 1 and itself. Examples: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.

points.label: Composite
points.text: A number with more than two factors. Examples: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers can't be divided except by 1 and themselves.

image.alt: Prime and Composite — Number Play

slides.title: Identifying Prime Numbers
slides.storyContext: Raj tries to divide 13 by 2, 3, 4... None work. 13 is prime!

example.problem: Is 15 prime or composite?
example.solution: 15 = 3 × 5, so it has factors 1, 3, 5, 15. It is composite.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide by small numbers; if nothing works except 1, it's prime.

image.alt: Identifying Prime Numbers — Number Play

slides.title: Number Detective
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj: find all prime numbers between 1 and 20, then find all multiples of 3.
slides.inSimpleWords: Use division rules to identify number patterns.

image.alt: Number Detective — Number Play

slides.title: Number Play Review
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj summarize: even/odd divide numbers, factors divide evenly, multiples come from skip-counting, primes are special.

points.label: Concepts
points.text: Even (÷2), Odd (÷2 with remainder), Factors (divide evenly), Multiples (skip-count).

points.label: Special Numbers
points.text: Prime (two factors), Composite (more than two factors).

slides.inSimpleWords: All numbers have patterns in how they divide and multiply.

image.alt: Number Play Review — Number Play

subject: Mathematics
title: The Prime Number Quest
hook: Raj and Meera discover which numbers stand alone and why they matter.

slides.title: Building Blocks
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj that every number is made of prime number building blocks, like atoms in chemistry.
slides.inSimpleWords: Prime numbers are nature's building blocks of all numbers.

image.alt: Building Blocks — Prime Time

slides.title: Prime Factorization
slides.storyContext: Raj breaks 12 into primes: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. He draws a tree showing how 12 splits into smaller primes.

points.label: Prime Factorization
points.text: Writing a number as a product of only prime numbers. Example: 12 = 2² × 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every number can be broken into prime number pieces.

image.alt: Prime Factorization — Prime Time

slides.title: Factor Trees
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj draw trees for different numbers, each ending in prime leaves.

example.problem: Find prime factorization of 30.
example.solution: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. Prime factorization: 2 × 3 × 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: Keep dividing by small primes until only primes remain.

image.alt: Factor Trees — Prime Time

slides.title: GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: Meera finds the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) and Least Common Multiple (LCM) using prime factors.

points.label: GCD
points.text: Greatest Common Divisor: largest number dividing both. Use shared prime factors.

points.label: LCM
points.text: Least Common Multiple: smallest number divisible by both. Use all prime factors.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD is the biggest shared divider, LCM is the smallest common multiple.

image.alt: GCD and LCM — Prime Time

slides.title: Finding GCD and LCM
slides.storyContext: Raj finds GCD and LCM of 12 and 18 using their prime factorizations.

example.problem: Find GCD and LCM of 12 and 18.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCD uses only shared primes, LCM uses all primes.

image.alt: Finding GCD and LCM — Prime Time

slides.title: Sieves and Prime Patterns
slides.storyContext: Meera shows the Sieve of Eratosthenes: crossing out multiples to find all primes up to 50.

points.label: Sieve Method
points.text: Cross out all multiples of each prime to find remaining primes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eliminate multiples to reveal all prime numbers.

image.alt: Sieves and Prime Patterns — Prime Time

slides.title: Prime Sieve Practice
slides.storyContext: Raj uses the sieve for numbers 1-30: mark 2, cross 4,6,8...; mark 3, cross 9,15,21...; mark 5, cross 25...

example.problem: Use Sieve of Eratosthenes to find primes up to 30.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mark each prime, cross out all its multiples.

image.alt: Prime Sieve Practice — Prime Time

slides.title: Prime Power Challenge
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Raj to find prime factorizations of 36 and 45, then their GCD.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: 36 = 2² × 3², 45 = 3² × 5. GCD = 9. Verify by division.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use prime factors to solve GCD and LCM puzzles.

image.alt: Prime Power Challenge — Prime Time

slides.title: Prime Time Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera recap: all numbers are built from primes, factor trees show the structure, GCD/LCM solve real problems.

points.label: Prime Factorization
points.text: Every number = unique product of primes.

points.label: GCD & LCM
points.text: Essential for fractions and problem-solving.

points.label: Sieves
points.text: Ancient method to find all primes in a range.

slides.inSimpleWords: Primes are nature's number building blocks.

image.alt: Prime Time Review — Prime Time

subject: Mathematics
title: Measuring Meera's Garden
hook: Meera plans to fence and paint her garden, learning perimeter and area.

slides.title: Garden Plans
slides.storyContext: Meera wants to fence her rectangular garden and paint the ground. She needs to know how much fence (perimeter) and paint (area).
slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter measures the distance around, area measures the space inside.

image.alt: Garden Plans — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: What is Perimeter?
slides.storyContext: Raj walks around Meera's garden boundary. The total distance he walks is the perimeter.

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Sum of all side lengths around a closed shape.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter is the distance around the outside of a shape.

image.alt: What is Perimeter? — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Perimeter of Rectangles
slides.storyContext: Meera's garden is 8 meters long and 5 meters wide. How much fencing does she need?

example.problem: Find perimeter of a rectangle with length 8 m and width 5 m.
example.solution: Perimeter = 2(length + width) = 2(8 + 5) = 2(13) = 26 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter of rectangle = 2 × (length + width).

image.alt: Perimeter of Rectangles — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: What is Area?
slides.storyContext: Meera measures how many square meter tiles fit in her garden. Each tile is 1m × 1m.

points.label: Area
points.text: Measure of space inside a closed shape, measured in square units.

slides.inSimpleWords: Area is how much space covers the shape.

image.alt: What is Area? — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Area of Rectangles
slides.storyContext: Meera's garden 8m × 5m is covered by 40 square tiles, each 1m × 1m.

example.problem: Find area of the same garden (8 m × 5 m).
example.solution: Area = length × width = 8 × 5 = 40 square meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Area of rectangle = length × width.

image.alt: Area of Rectangles — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Area of Other Shapes
slides.storyContext: Raj notices different garden shapes: triangular flower beds and circular fountain.

points.label: Triangle Area
points.text: Area = ½ × base × height.

points.label: Circle Area
points.text: Area = π × r² (where r is radius).

slides.inSimpleWords: Different shapes have different area formulas.

image.alt: Area of Other Shapes — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Mixed Shapes
slides.storyContext: A triangular flower bed has base 6m and height 4m. What is its area?

example.problem: Find area of triangle with base 6 m and height 4 m.
example.solution: Area = ½ × 6 × 4 = ½ × 24 = 12 square meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Triangle area is half of the rectangle with same base and height.

image.alt: Mixed Shapes — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Garden Redesign
slides.storyContext: Meera wants to expand her garden or change its shape. Raj calculates new perimeter and area.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: If Meera makes the garden 10m × 6m, new perimeter = 32m, new area = 60 sq.m.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use formulas to compare different garden sizes.

image.alt: Garden Redesign — Perimeter and Area

slides.title: Perimeter and Area Review
slides.storyContext: Meera buys fencing (perimeter) and paint (area) for her garden.

points.label: Perimeter
points.text: Sum of all sides; Rectangle = 2(l+w).

points.label: Area
points.text: Space inside; Rectangle = l×w, Triangle = ½bh.

points.label: Units
points.text: Perimeter in units (m), Area in square units (m²).

slides.inSimpleWords: Perimeter fences a garden, area paints its ground.

image.alt: Perimeter and Area Review — Perimeter and Area

subject: Mathematics
title: Sharing Pizza with Fractions
hook: Raj and Meera share a pizza and learn fractions the fun way.

slides.title: Pizza Division
slides.storyContext: A pizza arrives. Raj cuts it into 8 equal slices. He eats 3 slices. Meera says he ate 3/8 of the pizza.
slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions show parts of a whole.

image.alt: Pizza Division — Fractions

slides.title: Understanding Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera points out: 3 slices (numerator) out of 8 total slices (denominator).

points.label: Numerator
points.text: Top number: how many parts we have.

points.label: Denominator
points.text: Bottom number: how many equal parts the whole is divided into.

slides.inSimpleWords: Numerator is top (parts chosen), denominator is bottom (parts total).

image.alt: Understanding Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Types of Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj notices different slicing: 1/4 (one quarter), 1/2 (one half), 3/8 (three eighths).

example.problem: Classify 2/5, 5/5, 7/5 as proper, improper, or equal to 1.
example.solution: 2/5 is proper (less than 1). 5/5 equals 1. 7/5 is improper (more than 1).

slides.inSimpleWords: Proper < 1, improper ≥ 1. Mixed numbers combine whole + proper.

image.alt: Types of Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Equivalent Fractions
slides.storyContext: Meera cuts two pizzas differently: one into 4 slices (Raj eats 2 = 2/4), another into 8 slices (Meera eats 4 = 4/8). They ate the same amount!

points.label: Equivalent
points.text: Fractions that represent the same part of a whole. Example: 2/4 = 4/8.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different fractions can mean the same amount.

image.alt: Equivalent Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Simplifying Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj wonders if 6/9 can be simplified. Meera divides both by 3: 6/9 = 2/3.

example.problem: Simplify 12/16 to lowest terms.
example.solution: GCD(12,16) = 4. 12/16 = 3/4 (divide top and bottom by 4).

slides.inSimpleWords: Divide numerator and denominator by their GCD.

image.alt: Simplifying Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
slides.storyContext: Raj ate 1/4 pizza, Meera ate 2/4. Together they ate 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4.

points.label: Same Denominator
points.text: Add/subtract numerators, keep denominator: 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Same denominator: add/subtract tops, keep bottom same.

image.alt: Adding and Subtracting Fractions — Fractions

slides.title: Finding Common Denominators
slides.storyContext: Raj wants to add 1/3 + 1/4. Meera finds LCM(3,4) = 12: 1/3 = 4/12, 1/4 = 3/12, sum = 7/12.
slides.inSimpleWords: Find common denominator using LCM before adding.

image.alt: Finding Common Denominators — Fractions

slides.title: Pizza Math Challenge
slides.storyContext: Raj eats 3/8, Meera eats 2/8, their friend eats 1/8. What fraction remains?
slides.inSimpleWords: Use addition to find total, subtract from 1.

image.alt: Pizza Math Challenge — Fractions

slides.title: Fractions Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera finish their pizza lesson.

points.label: Basics
points.text: Numerator (parts chosen), Denominator (total parts).

points.label: Operations
points.text: Simplify using GCD, add/subtract using common denominators.

points.label: Real Use
points.text: Fractions describe sharing, measuring, cooking, time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fractions are ways to show parts of a whole.

image.alt: Fractions Review — Fractions

subject: Mathematics
title: Collecting School Survey Data
hook: Raj and Meera survey classmates to learn how to collect and display data.

slides.title: The Survey
slides.storyContext: Raj asks classmates: 'What is your favorite subject?' Meera organizes the answers: Math (8), Science (6), English (4), Hindi (5), Sports (7).
slides.inSimpleWords: Data is information we collect and organize.

image.alt: The Survey — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Collecting Data
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: data can come from surveys, observations, or measurements. Always ask clear questions.

points.label: Types of Data
points.text: Qualitative (colors, preferences), Quantitative (numbers, measurements).

slides.inSimpleWords: Data is facts and information collected carefully.

image.alt: Collecting Data — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Tallying and Frequency
slides.storyContext: Raj uses tally marks to count: Math |||||| || (8 votes), Science |||| | (6 votes).

example.problem: Make a frequency table for favorite colors: Red (7), Blue (9), Green (5), Yellow (4).
example.solution:
Color | Tally | Frequency
Red | |||||| | 7
Blue | |||||||| | 9
Green | ||||| | 5
Yellow | |||| | 4

slides.inSimpleWords: Tally marks and frequency tables organize counted data.

image.alt: Tallying and Frequency — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Pictographs and Bar Charts
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a bar chart: each bar's height shows how many votes each subject got.

points.label: Pictograph
points.text: Uses pictures to represent data; 1 picture = a fixed number of items.

points.label: Bar Chart
points.text: Uses rectangular bars to compare quantities across categories.

slides.inSimpleWords: Charts make data easy to see and compare at a glance.

image.alt: Pictographs and Bar Charts — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Making a Bar Chart
slides.storyContext: Raj draws the favorite subject bar chart: y-axis = number of votes (0-8), x-axis = subjects.

example.problem: Draw a bar chart for favorite sport: Cricket (10), Football (8), Basketball (6), Tennis (4).
example.solution: Bars rise to 10, 8, 6, 4 respectively. Cricket has the tallest bar, tennis the shortest.

slides.inSimpleWords: Height of bar = amount of data for that category.

image.alt: Making a Bar Chart — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Mean, Median, Mode
slides.storyContext: Meera analyzes the vote numbers: Mean (average), Median (middle), Mode (most common).

points.label: Mean
points.text: Sum of all values ÷ number of values.

points.label: Median
points.text: Middle value when arranged in order.

points.label: Mode
points.text: Value that appears most often.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean is average, median is middle, mode is most common.

image.alt: Mean, Median, Mode — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Finding Mean, Median, Mode
slides.storyContext: Vote counts: 8, 6, 4, 5, 7. Find mean, median, mode.

example.problem: Scores: 8, 6, 4, 5, 7. Find mean, median, mode.
example.solution: Mean = (8+6+4+5+7)÷5 = 30÷5 = 6. Median (ordered: 4,5,6,7,8) = 6. Mode = none (all appear once).

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean uses all values, median ignores outliers, mode shows preference.

image.alt: Finding Mean, Median, Mode — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Survey and Present
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Raj to survey 20 classmates on favorite games, make a bar chart, and find mean players per game.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Collect data → Tally → Frequency table → Bar chart → Calculate mean.

slides.inSimpleWords: Go from survey to organized chart to statistical analysis.

image.alt: Survey and Present — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Data Handling Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera review the complete data journey.

points.label: Collection
points.text: Ask clear questions, record carefully.

points.label: Organization
points.text: Frequency tables, pictographs, bar charts.

points.label: Analysis
points.text: Mean (average), Median (middle), Mode (most).

slides.inSimpleWords: Data tells stories when collected and presented clearly.

image.alt: Data Handling Review — Data Handling and Presentation

subject: Science
title: Raj's Nature Hike Classification
hook: Raj explores a nature trail and learns how scientists organize all living things.

slides.title: Nature Trail Discovery
slides.storyContext: During a hike, Raj spots plants, insects, birds, and mammals. Meera explains these are all organisms, but they're organized into different groups.
slides.inSimpleWords: Living things come in many different types.

image.alt: Nature Trail Discovery — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: What Makes Things Alive?
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj that all living things move, eat, grow, reproduce, and respond to their environment.

points.label: Characteristics
points.text: Growth, reproduction, response to environment, use of energy, homeostasis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Living things grow, move, reproduce, and respond to their world.

image.alt: What Makes Things Alive? — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Kingdom Kingdoms
slides.storyContext: Raj learns the five kingdoms: Animals (move, eat), Plants (make own food), Fungi (decompose), Protists (single-celled mostly), Bacteria (tiny, everywhere).

example.problem: Classify these as animal, plant, or fungus: dog, rice, mushroom, tree, ant.
example.solution: Dog and ant are animals. Rice and tree are plants. Mushroom is fungus.

slides.inSimpleWords: Five major kingdoms organize all life on Earth.

image.alt: Kingdom Kingdoms — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
slides.storyContext: Raj notices the bird has bones (backbone), but the butterfly doesn't. Meera explains vertebrates have spines, invertebrates don't.

points.label: Vertebrates
points.text: Have backbone: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.

points.label: Invertebrates
points.text: No backbone: insects, worms, crustaceans, mollusks, spiders.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertebrates have backbones, invertebrates don't.

image.alt: Vertebrates and Invertebrates — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Animal Classification
slides.storyContext: Raj sorts animals he sees: sparrow (bird), lizard (reptile), beetle (insect), frog (amphibian), fish (fish).

example.problem: Classify: whale, snake, octopus, cow, eagle.
example.solution: Whale and cow are mammals. Snake is reptile. Octopus is mollusk. Eagle is bird.

slides.inSimpleWords: Groups share features: birds have feathers, fish have gills, mammals feed milk.

image.alt: Animal Classification — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Plants: Different Types
slides.storyContext: Meera points out mosses (no roots), ferns (have roots but no seeds), and flowering plants (have seeds and flowers).

points.label: Mosses
points.text: Simple plants, no roots or seeds, reproduce by spores.

points.label: Ferns
points.text: Have roots and leaves, reproduce by spores.

points.label: Seed Plants
points.text: Flowering and cone-bearing plants, reproduce by seeds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants get more complex: mosses → ferns → seed plants.

image.alt: Plants: Different Types — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Finding Plant Types
slides.storyContext: Raj identifies moss on a rock, fern in shade, and flowers in sunlight on the trail.

example.problem: You find three plants: one very simple on wet rock, one with leaves but no flowers, one with bright flowers. Classify each.
example.solution: Rock plant is moss. Leafy plant is fern. Flowering plant is a seed plant (flowering plant).

slides.inSimpleWords: Observe roots, seeds, and leaves to identify plant types.

image.alt: Finding Plant Types — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Classify Your Neighborhood
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to list 10 organisms he sees at home and classify each by kingdom and type.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Note at least one animal, one plant, and one microorganism (like fungus bread mold).

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around and classify living things by their features.

image.alt: Classify Your Neighborhood — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Diversity Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera finish the hike, appreciating Earth's incredible variety of life.

points.label: Kingdoms
points.text: Animals, Plants, Fungi, Protists, Bacteria.

points.label: Animals
points.text: Vertebrates (backbone) or Invertebrates (no backbone).

points.label: Plants
points.text: Mosses, Ferns, or Seed Plants (simple to complex).

slides.inSimpleWords: Life's diversity is organized by shared features.

image.alt: Diversity Review — Diversity in the Living World

subject: Science
title: Meera's Magnetic Adventure
hook: Meera discovers invisible forces when magnets attract and repel around her home.

slides.title: Magnetic Discovery
slides.storyContext: Meera picks up iron nails with a magnet. Raj asks, 'Why do they stick?' Meera explains that magnets have invisible pulling power.
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are objects with invisible pulling and pushing forces.

image.alt: Magnetic Discovery — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: What is a Magnet?
slides.storyContext: Meera shows different magnets: bar magnet, horseshoe magnet, electromagnet. They all attract iron and steel.

points.label: Magnet
points.text: Object with magnetic field; attracts iron and steel; has poles (north and south).

slides.inSimpleWords: A magnet attracts certain metals without touching them.

image.alt: What is a Magnet? — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic
slides.storyContext: Meera tests objects: iron (attracted), aluminum foil (not attracted), steel (attracted), plastic (not attracted).

example.problem: Test these with a magnet: nail, rubber, coin, spoon, plastic bag.
example.solution: Nail and spoon attract (if metal). Rubber, coin, plastic bag don't attract.

slides.inSimpleWords: Iron, steel, and nickel are magnetic; most others are not.

image.alt: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Magnetic Poles
slides.storyContext: Meera labels a bar magnet: North pole (N) and South pole (S). She notices they attract but opposite poles repel each other.

points.label: Poles
points.text: Every magnet has North and South poles. Opposite poles attract, like poles repel.

slides.inSimpleWords: N and S poles attract each other. N-N or S-S repel.

image.alt: Magnetic Poles — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Attraction and Repulsion
slides.storyContext: Raj holds two bar magnets: N-S together (pull), N-N together (push). Meera explains the rule.

example.problem: Magnet A (N-S) and Magnet B (N-S). If A's north faces B's south, do they attract or repel?
example.solution: Opposite poles (N-S) attract each other.

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite poles attract, same poles push away.

image.alt: Attraction and Repulsion — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Magnetic Field
slides.storyContext: Meera sprinkles iron filings around a magnet. The filings arrange in a pattern, showing the invisible magnetic field.

points.label: Magnetic Field
points.text: Invisible region around a magnet where magnetic force acts.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic field is the invisible area where magnet's force works.

image.alt: Magnetic Field — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Observing Magnetic Fields
slides.storyContext: Iron filings create patterns around the magnet showing field lines radiating from poles.

example.problem: A magnet attracts a nail from 5 cm away. Is the nail in the magnetic field?
example.solution: Yes, the nail feels attraction from 5 cm away, so it's in the magnetic field region.

slides.inSimpleWords: If a magnet pulls something without touching, it's in the magnetic field.

image.alt: Observing Magnetic Fields — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Magnet Experiments
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to predict: will a magnet work through paper? Glass? Water? Test and explain.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Magnetic force passes through paper and glass but weakens. Water also allows force to pass.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic fields pass through many materials.

image.alt: Magnet Experiments — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Magnets Review
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj explore everyday magnets: in compasses, door latches, magnetic stickers.

points.label: Basics
points.text: Magnets attract iron/steel via invisible poles (N and S).

points.label: Rules
points.text: Opposite poles attract, like poles repel, field passes through materials.

points.label: Uses
points.text: Compasses, electromagnets, motors, toys, separation tools.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are forces that work through invisible fields.

image.alt: Magnets Review — Exploring Magnets

subject: Science
title: Raj's Running Track Measurements
hook: Raj measures distances and times his runs, learning to quantify motion.

slides.title: Track Day
slides.storyContext: Raj wants to know how far he runs and how fast. Meera brings measuring tape and stopwatch.
slides.inSimpleWords: Length tells us distance, time tells us how fast.

image.alt: Track Day — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Standard Units of Length
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: centimeter (cm), meter (m), kilometer (km). The meter is the standard unit.

points.label: Metric Units
points.text: mm (millimeter), cm (centimeter), m (meter), km (kilometer). 1 m = 100 cm.

slides.inSimpleWords: Meter is the main unit; 100 cm = 1 meter.

image.alt: Standard Units of Length — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Measuring Length
slides.storyContext: Raj measures the track: 100 meters long. Using a measuring tape, he records: 100.0 m.

example.problem: A track is 100 meters. Express in centimeters and kilometers.
example.solution: 100 m = 10,000 cm (multiply by 100). 100 m = 0.1 km (divide by 1,000).

slides.inSimpleWords: Convert between units: multiply or divide by 10s.

image.alt: Measuring Length — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Time Measurement
slides.storyContext: Meera uses a stopwatch to time Raj's run. She records seconds, minutes.

points.label: Units
points.text: Second (s), minute (min), hour (h). 1 min = 60 s, 1 hour = 60 min.

slides.inSimpleWords: Second is the main unit; 60 seconds = 1 minute.

image.alt: Time Measurement — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Calculating Speed
slides.storyContext: Raj runs 100 meters in 20 seconds. Meera calculates his speed: 100÷20 = 5 meters per second.

example.problem: Raj runs 100 m in 20 s. What is his speed?
example.solution: Speed = distance ÷ time = 100 m ÷ 20 s = 5 m/s (meters per second).

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed = distance traveled ÷ time taken.

image.alt: Calculating Speed — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Motion Concepts
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: motion is change in position. Speed is how fast, velocity includes direction.

points.label: Speed
points.text: How fast something moves: distance ÷ time.

points.label: Velocity
points.text: Speed with direction: '5 m/s north'.

points.label: Acceleration
points.text: Change in speed or direction: speeding up, slowing down.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed shows how fast, velocity includes direction.

image.alt: Motion Concepts — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Real Motion Scenarios
slides.storyContext: Raj experiments: walk at constant speed (slow), jog (medium), sprint (fast), then suddenly stop.

example.problem: Raj walks 30 m in 10 s, then runs 50 m in 10 s. Which is faster?
example.solution: Walk: 30÷10 = 3 m/s. Run: 50÷10 = 5 m/s. Running is faster.

slides.inSimpleWords: Faster motion covers more distance in same time.

image.alt: Real Motion Scenarios — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Motion Analysis
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to measure his friend's 200 m dash time and calculate speed.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: If 200 m in 40 s, then speed = 200÷40 = 5 m/s.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use stopwatch and measuring tape to find real speeds.

image.alt: Motion Analysis — Measurement of Length and Motion

slides.title: Length and Motion Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera review track measurements and motion calculations.

points.label: Length
points.text: Standard units: cm, m, km. Convert by multiplying/dividing by 10s.

points.label: Motion
points.text: Speed = distance ÷ time. Velocity includes direction.

points.label: Measurement Tools
points.text: Measuring tape for length, stopwatch for time.

slides.inSimpleWords: Measure distance with tape, time with stopwatch, calculate speed.

image.alt: Length and Motion Review — Measurement of Length and Motion

subject: Science
title: Meera's Thermometer Exploration
hook: Meera discovers how to measure temperature safely and accurately.

slides.title: Feeling Hot and Cold
slides.storyContext: Meera dunks her hand in cold water, then hot water. She realizes touch isn't precise. A thermometer measures temperature accurately.
slides.inSimpleWords: Temperature measures how hot or cold something is.

image.alt: Feeling Hot and Cold — Temperature and its Measurement

slides.title: What is Temperature?
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: temperature measures the kinetic energy of molecules. Hot = fast-moving molecules, cold = slow-moving.

points.label: Temperature
points.text: Measure of how fast atoms/molecules move. Higher temp = faster motion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hot things have fast-moving particles, cold things have slow ones.

image.alt: What is Temperature? — Temperature and its Measurement

slides.title: Thermometer Types
slides.storyContext: Raj finds three thermometers: mercury (traditional), alcohol (colored liquid), digital (electronic display).

points.label: Liquid Thermometers
points.text: Mercury or alcohol rises in tube as temperature increases.

points.label: Digital Thermometers
points.text: Electronic sensors display temperature as numbers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Thermometers measure temperature using rising liquid or electronics.

image.alt: Thermometer Types — Temperature and its Measurement

slides.title: Reading a Thermometer
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj how to read a liquid thermometer: find the top of the liquid column, read the number.

example.problem: A thermometer shows the liquid rising to the 37 line. What is the temperature?
example.solution: Temperature is 37°C (Celsius). Always read at the top of the liquid level, eye level.

slides.inSimpleWords: Read thermometer at the top of the liquid, at eye level.

image.alt: Reading a Thermometer — Temperature and its Measurement

slides.title: Temperature Scales
slides.storyContext: Meera explains two scales: Celsius (water freezes at 0°C, boils at 100°C) and Fahrenheit (32°F to 212°F).

points.label: Celsius
points.text: Used in India and most countries. Water freezes at 0°C, boils at 100°C.

points.label: Fahrenheit
points.text: Used in USA. Water freezes at 32°F, boils at 212°F.

slides.inSimpleWords: Celsius: 0° (freeze) to 100° (boil). Most countries use Celsius.

image.alt: Temperature Scales — Temperature and its Measurement

slides.title: Measuring Body Temperature
slides.storyContext: Meera takes her body temperature: the thermometer reads 37°C (normal and healthy).

example.problem: A person's body temperature is 37°C. Is this normal or is the person sick?
example.solution: 37°C is normal body temperature. Fever starts around 38°C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Normal body temperature is about 37°C.

image.alt: Measuring Body Temperature — Temperature and its Measurement

slides.title: Water Temperature States
slides.storyContext: Meera heats ice to water to steam: 0°C (ice), 25°C (room temp), 37°C (body), 100°C (boiling).

example.problem: At what temperature does ice melt? At what temperature does water boil?
example.solution: Ice melts at 0°C. Water boils at 100°C (at sea level).

slides.inSimpleWords: 0°C (freeze) is ice, 100°C (boil) is steam, between is liquid water.

image.alt: Water Temperature States — Temperature and its Measurement

slides.title: Temperature Recording
slides.storyContext: Raj records temperatures throughout the day: morning (20°C), noon (28°C), evening (22°C).

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Record indoor temperature at 3 times daily for a week. Graph the data.

slides.inSimpleWords: Observe and record temperature changes over time.

image.alt: Temperature Recording — Temperature and its Measurement

slides.title: Temperature Review
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj recap thermometer safety and accurate measurement.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Temperature measures particle motion (kinetic energy).

points.label: Measurement
points.text: Use thermometers (liquid or digital), read at eye level, at top of liquid.

points.label: Scale
points.text: Celsius: 0° (freeze), 37° (body), 100° (boil).

slides.inSimpleWords: Thermometers safely measure temperature on the Celsius scale.

image.alt: Temperature Review — Temperature and its Measurement

subject: Science
chapter: A Journey through States of Water
title: Water's Three Forms Quest
hook: Raj and Meera trace water's transformation through solid, liquid, and gas.

slides.title: Ice to Steam
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj ice in a freezer, liquid water in a glass, and steam from boiling water. Same thing, three forms!
slides.inSimpleWords: Water changes form at different temperatures.

image.alt: Ice to Steam — A Journey through States of Water

slides.title: Solid: Ice
slides.storyContext: Raj touches ice: hard, cold, keeps shape. Molecules are locked in place, vibrating only slightly.

points.label: Solid Water
points.text: Ice forms at 0°C or below. Molecules are tightly packed, don't move freely.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ice is solid: hard, heavy, keeps its shape.

image.alt: Solid: Ice — A Journey through States of Water

slides.title: Liquid: Water
slides.storyContext: Meera pours water: flows, takes shape of container, molecules slide past each other.

points.label: Liquid Water
points.text: Forms between 0°C and 100°C. Molecules move freely, giving water fluidity.

slides.inSimpleWords: Water is liquid: flows, takes container shape.

image.alt: Liquid: Water — A Journey through States of Water

slides.title: Gas: Steam
slides.storyContext: Boiling water produces steam: invisible gas where molecules fly freely through air.

points.label: Gaseous Water
points.text: Steam forms above 100°C. Molecules move very fast, spread out widely.

slides.inSimpleWords: Steam is gas: spreads everywhere, invisible.

image.alt: Gas: Steam — A Journey through States of Water

slides.title: Melting and Freezing
slides.storyContext: Raj watches ice melt to water (melting) and water freeze to ice (freezing).

example.problem: Ice at 0°C warms to 50°C. What happens?
example.solution: At 0°C ice melts to water. As temp rises to 50°C, water stays liquid and gets warmer.

slides.inSimpleWords: Melting: solid → liquid. Freezing: liquid → solid.

image.alt: Melting and Freezing — A Journey through States of Water

slides.title: Evaporation and Condensation
slides.storyContext: Meera leaves wet clothes in sun; they dry (evaporation). Morning dew appears on grass (condensation).

points.label: Evaporation
points.text: Liquid water turns to steam/vapor, especially in heat.

points.label: Condensation
points.text: Water vapor cools and turns back to liquid (like foggy mirror).

slides.inSimpleWords: Evaporation: liquid → gas. Condensation: gas → liquid.

image.alt: Evaporation and Condensation — A Journey through States of Water

slides.title: Water Cycle Journey
slides.storyContext: Raj traces the cycle: sun evaporates ocean water (vapor) → rises and cools → condenses into clouds → falls as rain → flows to ocean.

example.problem: Trace the water cycle: sun heats ocean, clouds form, rain falls.
example.solution: Evaporation (sun heats water) → Condensation (vapor cools to clouds) → Precipitation (rain falls) → Runoff (returns to ocean).

slides.inSimpleWords: Water evaporates (rises), condenses (clouds), falls as rain, returns to ocean.

image.alt: Water Cycle Journey — A Journey through States of Water

slides.title: State Transitions
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj: at what temperature does each transition occur?

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Melting: 0°C. Boiling: 100°C. Freezing: 0°C. Condensation occurs below boiling point.

slides.inSimpleWords: Learn the key temperatures: 0° (solid ↔ liquid) and 100° (liquid ↔ gas).

image.alt: State Transitions — A Journey through States of Water

slides.title: States of Water Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera recap the journey: ice, water, steam, and the cycle that sustains all life.

points.label: Solid (Ice)
points.text: Below 0°C. Hard, fixed shape, molecules locked.

points.label: Liquid (Water)
points.text: 0°C to 100°C. Flows, takes shape, molecules move freely.

points.label: Gas (Steam)
points.text: Above 100°C. Invisible, spreads out, molecules very fast.

points.label: Cycle
points.text: Evaporation → Condensation → Precipitation → Runoff.

slides.inSimpleWords: Water cycles through solid, liquid, and gas forms, powering Earth's weather.

image.alt: States of Water Review — A Journey through States of Water

subject: Science
title: Meera's Material Detective Adventure
hook: Meera investigates the materials in her classroom and home, discovering their properties.

slides.title: Classroom Materials
slides.storyContext: Meera looks around: wood desk, metal chair, plastic bottle, glass window, paper book. Each material behaves differently.
slides.inSimpleWords: Everything is made of different materials with unique properties.

image.alt: Classroom Materials — Materials Around Us

slides.title: What are Materials?
slides.storyContext: Raj asks, 'What's a material?' Meera explains: materials are substances with specific properties, like hardness, color, and flexibility.

points.label: Material
points.text: Substance from which objects are made. Each has unique properties (hardness, color, texture, flexibility).

slides.inSimpleWords: Materials are what things are made from.

image.alt: What are Materials? — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Types of Materials
slides.storyContext: Meera sorts materials: metals (iron, aluminum), plastics (bottles, bags), ceramics (clay, tiles), wood, glass, rubber.

example.problem: Classify these by material type: iron nail, plastic cup, clay pot, wooden spoon, glass plate.
example.solution: Nail: metal. Cup: plastic. Pot: ceramic. Spoon: wood. Plate: glass.

slides.inSimpleWords: Common materials: metal, plastic, ceramic, wood, glass, rubber.

image.alt: Types of Materials — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Natural and Synthetic
slides.storyContext: Meera observes: cotton (natural), wool (natural), plastic (synthetic), steel (synthetic from iron ore).

points.label: Natural
points.text: Come from nature: cotton, wool, silk, wood, leather, rubber.

points.label: Synthetic
points.text: Made by humans: plastic, nylon, polyester, steel, concrete.

slides.inSimpleWords: Natural materials from nature, synthetic materials made by humans.

image.alt: Natural and Synthetic — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Properties of Materials
slides.storyContext: Raj tests: metal spoon conducts heat (conductor), plastic spoon doesn't (insulator). Glass breaks (brittle), rubber stretches (elastic).

example.problem: Which is best for a handle: metal, plastic, or wood? Why?
example.solution: Plastic or wood: they're insulators (don't conduct heat/cold) and have some flex. Metal conducts heat and can burn hands.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different materials have different usefulness for different jobs.

image.alt: Properties of Materials — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Physical Properties
slides.storyContext: Meera lists physical properties: hardness, transparency, flexibility, electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity, density.

points.label: Hardness
points.text: Diamond is very hard, lead is soft.

points.label: Transparency
points.text: Glass is transparent, wood is opaque.

points.label: Conductivity
points.text: Metals conduct electricity well, plastic doesn't.

slides.inSimpleWords: Properties describe how materials behave and look.

image.alt: Physical Properties — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Choosing Materials
slides.storyContext: Raj selects materials for tasks: metal for cooking pots (conducts heat), plastic for water bottles (doesn't rust), glass for windows (transparent).

example.problem: You need a material for an electric wire. Choose metal, plastic, or wood. Why?
example.solution: Metal: conducts electricity well. Plastic or wood: insulators, used as wire sheath.

slides.inSimpleWords: Match material properties to what you need.

image.alt: Choosing Materials — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Material Hunt
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to find 8 objects at home, identify the material, and list one key property.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Example: spoon (metal, conducts heat), cup (ceramic, hard), pen (plastic, flexible).

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around and identify materials and their properties.

image.alt: Material Hunt — Materials Around Us

slides.title: Materials Review
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj finish their material journey, appreciating how material science shapes everyday objects.

points.label: Types
points.text: Metal, plastic, ceramic, wood, glass, rubber, natural, synthetic.

points.label: Properties
points.text: Hardness, transparency, conductivity, flexibility, density.

points.label: Selection
points.text: Match material properties to the job needed.

slides.inSimpleWords: The right material for the right job makes everything work better.

image.alt: Materials Review — Materials Around Us
